title: The Stolen Blessing
summary: Old and nearly blind, Isaac sends Esau to hunt game so that he may bless him. Rebekah overhears, dresses Jacob in Esau's clothes and goatskins, and sends him in with a meal, and Jacob lies his way into the blessing of the firstborn. When Esau returns, Isaac trembles, and Esau weeps for a blessing of his own, receiving only a bleak word. Esau vows to kill Jacob, and Rebekah arranges for Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran.
story: God had told Rebekah before the twins were born that “the older will serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23), and Jacob had already bought Esau's birthright (25:29-34). Now the blessing itself is at stake: the father's solemn word that would carry the promises of Abraham to the next generation. Isaac intends to give it to Esau anyway. Every member of the family acts on their own plan, and the result is exactly what God had said, reached by the worst possible road. The chapter drives Jacob out of the land of promise, begins twenty years of exile, and sets the brothers at enmity. Jacob's story from here on is shaped by what he did in this tent.
historical:
Isaac believes he is near death, but Genesis later records that he lived to 180 (Genesis 35:28), so he survives for many years after this scene. In Israel and its neighbors a father's solemn blessing, especially near the end of life, was treated as effective and binding, a spoken act rather than a mere wish. Jacob will do the same for his own sons and grandsons in Genesis 48-49.

Isaac's words to Esau look ahead to the history of Edom, the nation descended from him, in the rugged country southeast of the Dead Sea. Edom was later brought under Israel's rule by David (2 Samuel 8:13-14) and broke free in the reign of Jehoram of Judah in the ninth century BC (2 Kings 8:20-22), matching the words, “when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck” (verse 40). The enmity between the two peoples runs through the prophets, notably Obadiah, and into the bitter memory of Edom's conduct when Jerusalem fell to Babylon (Psalm 137:7).
cultural:
The blessing of the firstborn was more than affection. It passed on leadership of the family and, in this family, the covenant promises: fertility of the land, rule over nations and brothers, and the words “May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed” (verse 29), which echo God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3. Once spoken in the presence of the LORD, it could not simply be taken back. When Isaac realizes what has happened, he says, “he will be blessed,” accepting that the word has gone out.

The deception depends on the senses of a blind old man. Isaac is asked to trust taste (a dish of goat prepared to taste like game), touch (goatskins on Jacob's smooth hands and neck), and smell (Esau's clothes, with their scent of the field), against the one sense that tells the truth: hearing. A mother's authority over a grown son is also on display. Jacob raises only the practical objection that he might be caught, and Rebekah answers, “Your curse be on me, my son.”
literary: The chapter unfolds in a series of scenes, each with only two characters on stage: Isaac and Esau, Rebekah and Jacob, Isaac and Jacob, Isaac and Esau, Rebekah and Jacob, Rebekah and Isaac. The family never appears together, and that absence is part of the story. Isaac's line, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (verse 22), captures the tension of the central scene. Isaac's blessings of Jacob and of Esau are poetry, and the second mirrors the first in reverse: the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth are given to Jacob, and Esau's dwelling will be away from them. The chapter plants seeds that grow later. Jacob uses a goat and his brother's garment to deceive his father; his own sons will use a goat and Joseph's garment to deceive him (Genesis 37:31-33). Jacob exploits being the younger; Laban will trick him with the older daughter (Genesis 29:26). Rebekah says she will send for Jacob when Esau calms down, but Genesis never records her seeing him again.

outline.t: Rebekah's plan to put Jacob in Esau's place
Jacob deceives Isaac and receives the blessing
Esau's bitter cry and his father's word
Esau's vow of revenge; Rebekah sends Jacob away

doctrines.note: God's announced purpose (Genesis 25:23) comes to pass, but not because anyone in the family trusts him to bring it about. God accomplishes his plan through, and despite, the schemes of sinful people, without approving their sin. Joseph will later state the principle: people meant evil, God meant good (Genesis 50:20).

Everyone is compromised. Isaac tries to bless Esau against God's word; Rebekah plans the deception; Jacob lies to his blind father and invokes God to cover the lie (verse 20); Esau, who despised his birthright, now weeps for the blessing and plans murder. The chapter lets each sin bear its own fruit.

Favoritism divides the household into rival camps, and the family ends scattered: one son in flight, one plotting murder, a mother who loses the son she favored. Genesis tells family life honestly, and this household's wounds will take decades to heal.

words.note: Berakah, blessing: a spoken gift of good, especially life, fruitfulness, and success, conveyed by one with authority to give it. In Genesis, blessing is God's intention for humanity from the first chapter (1:28). Esau's cry, “Do you have only one blessing, my father?” (verse 38), is one of the most painful lines in the book.

Mirmah, deceit or treachery. Isaac tells Esau, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing” (verse 35). The related verb appears when Jacob confronts Laban over the switched bride (Genesis 29:25), and the noun again when Jacob's sons answer the men of Shechem (34:13): deceit keeps returning to this family.

Aqav, to grasp by the heel, to overreach or cheat. Esau makes a bitter pun on his brother's name: “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me twice” (verse 36). The heel-grabber of the birth story has become a supplanter.

Nakar, to recognize. Isaac “did not recognize him” (verse 23). Recognition, and failure to recognize, becomes a thread through the rest of Genesis: Jacob is asked to recognize Joseph's bloodied robe (37:32-33), Judah to recognize his own seal (38:25-26), and Joseph recognizes his brothers who don't recognize him (42:7-8).

christ: Hebrews 11:20 says that “By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future.” However flawed the scene, Isaac's words carried God's promise forward, and he held to them once spoken. The blessing Jacob receives includes the Abrahamic promise that those who bless him will be blessed and those who curse him cursed, and it continues the line through which blessing for all nations will come in Christ. Hebrews 12:16-17 also uses Esau, who later sought the blessing with tears, as a warning against treating God's gifts lightly. Some Christian interpreters have seen an analogy in Jacob receiving the blessing clothed in his elder brother's garments, since believers are blessed clothed in Christ (Galatians 3:27). The analogy has limits, and the contrast teaches more than the likeness: Jacob stole his brother's place by lies, while Christ freely gives his place to those who have no claim on it.

hard.q: If God had promised the blessing to Jacob, why does it come through lies, and does God approve?
hard.a:
Genesis doesn't say that the deception was right, and it shows the cost in detail. Jacob loses his home for twenty years, is deceived in turn by Laban, and lives in fear of his brother; Rebekah loses the son she loved; Esau is left bitter; and the family's pattern of deceit reaches into the next generation. God had already spoken (Genesis 25:23), so the scheme was not needed to secure the promise. Like Sarah's plan with Hagar, it was an attempt to seize by human cunning what God had pledged to give.

Interpreters weigh the characters differently. Some see Rebekah as acting in faith on the oracle, however wrongly she went about it, and Isaac as the one resisting God's word by favoring Esau; others stress that all four are culpable. Most agree on the larger point: the Bible does not make its heroes into models of virtue. It shows God keeping his promise through people who don't deserve it, and it lets their sins bring real consequences. God's faithfulness is not a reward for their faithfulness, and that is precisely what makes it grace.

questions: Every member of this family tried to control the outcome. Where are you tempted to take matters into your own hands instead of trusting God's timing?
Isaac trusted his touch, taste, and smell over the voice he heard. When have you believed what you wanted to believe despite clear signs to the contrary?
Jacob will spend years reaping what he sowed here. How do you hold together God's grace and the real consequences of our choices?
